points: Artistic activities give learners creative crafting and performance of activities.
They involve imaginative combinations of skills, techniques and/or movements.
The combinations are performed in the appropriate style of the event.
Aesthetic activities give learners the opportunity to demonstrate appreciation of the qualities of movement.
They also show appreciation of the expressive abilities of the performers.
Learners demonstrate this by adopting aesthetic criteria when they plan, perform and evaluate the activity.
The area offers artistic gymnastics, rhythmic gymnastics and dance.
Dance may be in any one of eight styles: contemporary, folk, modern, ballet, jazz, tap, ethnic or traditional.
One activity from this area may be one of the student's three.

notes.h: Links to compositional elements and criteria
points: Routines are built from compositional elements: action, space, dynamics, relationships and choreographic form.
Routines are judged against aesthetic and artistic criteria: body line, control, fluency, musicality, expression and originality.
Example: a planned change from high to low levels uses the space element, and a balance held still with a clean finish shows control.

notes.h: Safe practice in gymnastics and dance
points: The warm-up includes mobility work before skills are attempted.
Skills are taught through correct progressions, with each simpler step secured before the next is attempted.
In gymnastics, spotting and supporting are used when a skill needs them.
Mats are positioned and checked, and apparatus is checked before use.
No jewellery is worn and hair is tied back.
Dance requires a suitable floor surface.
Hydration is part of safe practice.
Overuse is avoided to prevent injury.
Assessment covers the listed skills performed within a routine or dance.
It also covers compositional and choreographic knowledge.
Rules of the activity and safe practice are assessed.
Performances are captured on video.
In written exams, aesthetic activities are used to test aesthetic and artistic criteria, compositional elements, methods of analysing choreography and the comparison of two activities.

keyTerms.definition: An activity in which learners create and perform imaginative combinations of skills, techniques and/or movements in the appropriate style of the event.
An activity in which learners appreciate the qualities of movement and the expressive abilities of performers, using aesthetic criteria.
The standards used to plan, perform and evaluate a routine, such as body line, control, fluency, musicality, expression and originality.
The building blocks of a routine: action, space, dynamics, relationships and choreographic form.
The overall structure of a dance or routine, showing how its sections are arranged.
A sequence of simpler steps leading to a harder skill, with each step secured before the next is attempted.
Physically guiding or supporting a performer through a skill to prevent a fall or injury.
An injury caused by repeated loading of the same body part without enough recovery.
A sequence of movements or skills performed as one continuous piece.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between artistic and aesthetic activities, giving an example from gymnastics or dance.
questions.model: An artistic activity gives learners creative crafting and performance: they combine skills, techniques and/or movements imaginatively, in the appropriate style of the event. An aesthetic activity gives learners the opportunity to appreciate the qualities of movement and the expressive abilities of performers, and learners use aesthetic criteria to plan, perform and evaluate it. Example from gymnastics: a gymnast who designs a new combination of skills and movements for a floor routine, and performs it in the style of artistic gymnastics, is working in an artistic activity. Example from dance: a learner who watches a classmate's dance and judges its fluency, body line and expression against aesthetic criteria is demonstrating appreciation of the quality of the movement, which is the aesthetic focus.

questions.prompt: Outline three safe-practice measures in gymnastics.
questions.model: First, a warm-up that includes mobility work is completed before any skill is attempted, so the joints and muscles are prepared. Second, correct progressions are followed, with each simpler step secured before a harder one is tried, and spotting and supporting are used where a skill needs them. Third, the mats are positioned and checked and the apparatus is checked before use, and performers wear no jewellery and tie back their hair.
